strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and useful problem: real-world aerial semantic scene completion. A benchmark with RGB images, semantic occupancy grids, and metric depth maps from UAV viewpoints would be valuable for vision-based 3D perception beyond autonomous driving.

The proposed camera-based data generation pipeline is practically motivated for UAVs, where LiDAR payload, power, and regulatory constraints are real issues. The use of SfM/MVS correspondences to lift a small number of 2D annotations into 3D is a sensible and scalable design.

The dataset is reasonably substantial for a new domain: 9 scenes, 20,160 samples, three altitudes, 22 classes, and approximately 194k square meters across rural, urban, and industrial settings and multiple seasons.

The manuscript provides useful implementation details in the supplement, including voxel resolution, DBSCAN parameters, class groupings, annotation ratios, hardware, and model training setup. This improves reproducibility relative to many dataset papers.

The depth estimation evaluation is a useful extra contribution. Fine-tuning Depth Anything V2 on OccuFly yields large improvements over an out-of-domain metric model, supporting the claim that aerial metric depth has a meaningful domain gap.
weaknesses: The central weakness is ground-truth validation. The paper treats SfM/MVS reconstruction plus densification as ground truth, but provides no independent geometric accuracy evaluation against LiDAR, survey-grade checkpoints, manually checked voxels, or held-out depth measurements. Reprojection RMSE is not sufficient to establish occupancy, depth, or volumetric completeness accuracy.

Semantic label quality is also insufficiently validated. The pipeline relies on annotating fewer than 10% of images, majority voting, kNN propagation, DBSCAN, Poisson reconstruction, and visual hull carving, but there is no quantitative audit of propagated 3D labels or voxel labels against manually verified 3D/2D holdouts. Qualitative figures alone do not support claims of high fidelity.

The benchmark evaluation for SSC is narrow: only CGFormer is evaluated. There are no simple baselines, no comparisons to other representative SSC methods, no ablations of depth priors or altitude-specific training, and no analysis separating model failure from potential label/pipeline artifacts.

The reported SSC performance is extremely low, with all-altitude mIoU around 0.008 and many classes at zero IoU. This does show difficulty, but it also raises concerns about whether the task formulation, labels, class taxonomy, or train/test split are suitable. The paper does not sufficiently diagnose this failure mode.

The class distribution is severely imbalanced, with building occupying about 75.7% of semantic voxels and several classes below 0.01%. Some rare classes such as person and flying animal appear nearly absent, making the effective 22-class benchmark much weaker than the taxonomy suggests.

Dataset diversity is still limited despite the sample count: only 9 scenes from a single geographic region. The train/validation/test split may test scene-level generalization, but it does not strongly support claims of broad aerial-domain generality.

The generation of 40 m and 30 m ground truth by frustum-culling the 50 m scene-level semantic voxel grid weakens the claim of independent multi-altitude annotation and may obscure altitude-specific reconstruction/labeling errors. The authors acknowledge temporal inconsistencies, but the impact is not quantified.

Reproducibility is partially limited by reliance on proprietary Agisoft Metashape and by the statement that code/data will be released upon acceptance rather than being available for review. Key implementation details such as exact voxel carving, mesh-to-voxel conversion, and annotation tooling may be hard to reproduce from the paper alone.

Several claims are overstated. For example, low reprojection error is described as validating high metric accuracy and as a proxy for depth accuracy, but reprojection error can be low despite scale, surface, or occlusion errors in dense reconstruction. Claims that densification removes holes in final volumetric ground truth are not quantitatively supported.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful gap: semantic scene completion from low-altitude aerial imagery is much less explored than terrestrial autonomous-driving SSC, and a real-world camera-based benchmark could be useful to the community.

The proposed dataset has several potentially valuable assets: 20,160 RGB samples, per-frame depth maps, semantic voxel grids, multiple altitudes, oblique/nadir views, seasonal variation, and 22 classes in an SSCBench-like format.
The manuscript gives a reasonably clear end-to-end pipeline for SfM/MVS reconstruction, 2D mask annotation, 2D-to-3D label lifting, densification, voxelization, and per-frame frustum extraction.
The paper includes initial baselines for both aerial SSC and metric monocular depth estimation, which helps establish that existing models struggle in this domain.
weaknesses: The central weakness is insufficient validation of the generated ground truth. The paper relies mainly on SfM/MVS reprojection error and qualitative visualizations, but reprojection error is not a reliable proxy for metric depth accuracy, semantic voxel accuracy, completeness, or correctness of occluded geometry. There is no comparison against LiDAR, surveyed control points, manually checked 3D labels, held-out dense annotations, or other independent reference data.

The label-generation pipeline introduces several sources of potentially consequential error that are not quantified: sparse 2D annotation propagated by majority voting, kNN relabeling of all points, DBSCAN instance separation, alpha-shape visual hull carving, Poisson reconstruction for ground classes, and fixed precedence rules during voxel aggregation. These steps can hallucinate geometry and semantics, especially in texture-poor regions, thin structures, rare classes, vegetation, cables, and occlusions.

The benchmark evidence is weak. Only one SSC model, CGFormer, is evaluated, and the reported SSC performance is extremely low: all-altitude mIoU is 0.0080 with many classes at exactly or nearly zero IoU. This demonstrates difficulty, but it does not provide a strong benchmark characterization or enough evidence that the task setup, labels, and evaluation protocol are robust.

Dataset breadth is limited despite the large sample count. The data come from only 9 scenes within a single geographic region, and the semantic distribution is highly imbalanced, with buildings comprising about 75.7% of voxels while many classes are below 0.01%. Several of the 22 classes therefore appear too rare for meaningful learning or evaluation.

The claim of scalable annotation is not fully supported. The paper reports that less than 10% of images cover more than 99% of reconstructed points, but coverage of reconstructed points is not the same as semantic correctness, boundary accuracy, or voxel-level label quality. There is no reported annotator agreement, annotation QA protocol, or quantitative audit of lifted labels.

The depth-map contribution is also under-validated. The metric depth maps are derived from the same photogrammetric reconstruction whose accuracy is only indirectly assessed. Fine-tuning Depth Anything V2 on these maps and evaluating on the same derived-label distribution mainly shows in-domain fitting, not necessarily reliable metric depth supervision.

There are reproducibility concerns. The reconstruction depends on proprietary Agisoft Metashape and many implementation choices and hyperparameters. The paper states that data/code will be released upon acceptance, but the current manuscript does not demonstrate that an external researcher could reproduce the dataset generation or verify the labels.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, including statements such as densification removing reconstruction holes in the final ground truth and reprojection error validating depth accuracy. These are important assumptions, not demonstrated results.

The split and acquisition design raise concerns: 30 m and 40 m ground truth is generated by frustum-culling a 50 m scene-level grid, and the authors acknowledge possible temporal inconsistency across altitudes. This could create mismatches between images and labels, but the magnitude of the issue is not measured.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear gap: semantic scene completion from aerial/UAV viewpoints is underexplored, and a real-world camera-based benchmark is a useful contribution for computer vision and robotics.

OccuFly appears substantial in scope: 20,160 samples, 9 scenes, three altitudes, multiple seasons/scenario types, 22 semantic classes, semantic occupancy grids, and metric depth maps. The dataset format is aligned with existing SSC conventions, which should lower adoption friction.

The proposed LiDAR-free data generation pipeline is well motivated for UAV constraints. Using SfM/MVS correspondences to lift sparse 2D annotations into 3D is a practical and potentially scalable approach, and the paper gives concrete implementation details such as annotation sampling, kNN propagation, DBSCAN parameters, Poisson reconstruction settings, voxel resolution, and hardware.

The manuscript includes meaningful dataset diagnostics: reprojection RMSE, annotation ratios, class frequencies, scene statistics, depth-map comparisons, qualitative point-cloud/voxel visualizations, and benchmark results for both SSC and metric monocular depth estimation.

The benchmark experiments reveal that current terrestrial SSC methods perform very poorly in this aerial setting, which supports the paper's claim that OccuFly exposes a real domain gap and can motivate future method development.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with a transparent limitations section acknowledging static-scene assumptions, cross-altitude temporal inconsistencies, and remaining manual labeling effort.
weaknesses: The most important concern is ground-truth validity. The paper relies heavily on SfM/MVS reprojection error and qualitative visualizations as evidence, but does not provide independent validation against LiDAR, ground control/check points, dense manual 3D labels, or a held-out manual voxel/point audit. Low reprojection error is not sufficient to establish semantic occupancy accuracy, especially after kNN propagation, Poisson filling, and silhouette/visual-hull densification.

The densification pipeline can introduce hallucinated geometry and semantic artifacts: Poisson reconstruction for ground classes enforces continuity, visual-hull carving can overfill instances, and kNN smoothing may propagate labels across object boundaries. The paper claims these steps remove reconstruction holes, but does not quantitatively evaluate the error they introduce or ablate their impact.

The SSC benchmarking is narrow. Only CGFormer is evaluated for SSC, and its resulting semantic performance is extremely low (overall mIoU around 0.008), making it hard to understand whether the benchmark is learnable, whether failures come from the model, the depth prior, the aerial viewpoint, or label noise. Additional baselines or simpler diagnostic models would strengthen the evidence.

The dataset diversity is valuable but still limited: only 9 scenes from a single geographic region, with test scenes likely sharing acquisition pipelines, platforms, and environmental context. This may limit claims about broad aerial-scene generalization.

The class distribution is highly imbalanced, with buildings dominating roughly 75% of voxels and many classes essentially absent. Rare categories such as persons, flying animals, cables, cranes, and bicycles have near-zero frequency, so their inclusion in a 22-class taxonomy may overstate practical semantic coverage and makes class-wise mIoU difficult to interpret.

Ground truth at 40 m and 30 m is generated by frustum-culling the 50 m scene-level semantic voxel grid. This is efficient, but it weakens the independence of altitude-specific labels and may be problematic when cross-altitude captures have temporal differences, viewpoint-specific reconstruction failures, or dynamic objects.

The metric depth evaluation is useful, but the comparison to off-the-shelf DAv2-metric is somewhat expected because DAv2-OccuFly is fine-tuned in-domain. The depth maps themselves also inherit SfM/MVS assumptions, and their metric accuracy is not independently validated beyond reprojection error.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully guaranteed from the manuscript alone: code and dataset release are stated as future/upon acceptance, data generation depends on proprietary Agisoft Metashape, and withheld locations plus possible licensing/privacy constraints could affect full reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear gap: semantic scene completion from low-altitude aerial imagery is underexplored, and the proposed OccuFly benchmark is positioned as the first real-world aerial SSC dataset with RGB images, semantic voxel grids, and metric depth maps.

The data generation pipeline is technically coherent and well motivated for UAV constraints: SfM/MVS reconstruction, sparse manual 2D annotation, multi-view label lifting, class-aware densification, voxelization, frustum-culling, and SemanticKITTI-style masks form a plausible end-to-end route to SSC supervision without LiDAR.

The dataset is substantial for a new domain benchmark: 20,611 samples, 9 scenes, roughly 194k square meters, 3 altitudes, 21 classes, multiple environment types, and all seasons. The comparison to existing SSC and aerial depth datasets supports its practical novelty.

The manuscript provides useful validation evidence, including reprojection errors, annotation ratios, image overlap analysis, qualitative scene-level reconstructions, and an additional semantic/geometric check reporting 92% pixel-wise agreement on 135 held-out manual annotations.

The benchmark experiments are appropriate for establishing task difficulty rather than claiming state-of-the-art modeling. Results on Symphonies, DISC, and several metric depth foundation models show a large aerial domain gap and make a reasonable case that the dataset can stimulate further research.

The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes many implementation details in the supplement, including reconstruction software, kNN parameters, DBSCAN parameters, voxel grid specification, splits, and class frequencies.
weaknesses: Ground-truth validity is the main concern. The paper relies heavily on SfM/MVS outputs and reprojection error as evidence of geometric accuracy, but reprojection error is only an indirect proxy for dense metric depth and occupancy correctness. There is no comparison to independent ground truth such as LiDAR scans, surveyed control points, manually inspected depth samples, or cross-sensor validation.

The semantic validation is under-specified relative to the strength of the dataset claims. The reported 92% pixel-wise agreement on rendered semantic point clouds is encouraging, but pixel accuracy can be dominated by frequent classes, especially with buildings at about 62% overall and 75% in the test distribution. Per-class IoU, confusion matrices, and separate analysis for rare/small objects would be much more diagnostic.

The 21-class taxonomy appears ambitious, but many classes are extremely rare, including person, bicycle, cable, crane, and cable tower. Baseline SSC results are zero or near-zero for many of these classes, raising questions about whether the dataset meaningfully supports learning and evaluation for the full label set.

The dataset diversity is useful but still geographically limited: all scenes are from the broader Ingolstadt region, with only 9 scenes. Train/validation/test splits may entangle location, season, environment, and platform differences, making it hard to isolate generalization factors or know how well conclusions transfer to other cities, countries, architectures, and vegetation types.

The benchmark coverage is somewhat narrow for SSC. Only two SSC methods are evaluated, and both are terrestrial methods adapted with a fine-tuned depth model. This is sufficient to expose difficulty, but it provides a limited picture of how other occupancy paradigms, multi-view variants, or simpler geometry/depth baselines behave on OccuFly.

The data generation includes several heuristic choices that may introduce systematic artifacts: DBSCAN instance separation, visual-hull densification, Poisson reconstruction for ground classes, class-prior tie breaking, kNN relabeling, fixed precedence ordering, and using a 50 m scene-level grid to generate lower-altitude ground truth. The paper gives parameters, but limited ablations quantify how these choices affect final voxel labels.

Temporal consistency is acknowledged as a limitation, but it is potentially material: data across altitudes may be captured at different times while lower-altitude samples are generated from a common scene grid. This can affect dynamic objects and scene changes, especially for vehicles, people, construction, and seasonal vegetation.

Reproducibility is partly constrained by reliance on proprietary Agisoft Metashape for reconstruction and by the absence, in the manuscript itself, of a clear release checklist for all generated labels, scripts, splits, and annotation protocols. The dataset may still be usable, but reproducing the full pipeline could be difficult.

strengths: The paper targets a real gap: semantic scene completion from low-altitude aerial imagery is underexplored compared with autonomous driving, and a real-world aerial SSC benchmark could be useful to the community.

The dataset has nontrivial scale and scope: 9 scenes, 20,611 image/grid/depth samples, 21 semantic classes, three altitudes, and rural/urban/industrial scenes across seasons. The paper also provides depth maps, masks, and a data organization intended to be compatible with existing SSC pipelines.

The proposed annotation-transfer pipeline is practical and potentially valuable. Annotating 586 images, about 9.17% of acquired images, and lifting labels via multi-view correspondences is a reasonable way to reduce manual 3D labeling effort.

The paper includes meaningful baseline experiments for two SSC models and several metric depth models. The results clearly show that terrestrial SSC models and zero-shot monocular depth models perform poorly in this aerial setting, motivating the benchmark.
The manuscript is generally well organized, with dataset statistics, class frequencies, annotation ratios, reconstruction reprojection errors, and supplementary implementation details.
weaknesses: The central weakness is that the benchmark ground truth is not validated strongly enough. The SSC labels are generated from SfM/MVS, label lifting, kNN smoothing, Poisson reconstruction, visual-hull densification, and hand-chosen precedence rules, but there is no independent 3D validation against LiDAR, surveyed geometry, dense manual 3D annotation, or another external measurement source. For a benchmark paper, this substantially undermines confidence in the occupancy labels.

The reported validation metrics do not fully establish semantic occupancy correctness. A mean reprojection error of 1.24 px mainly measures photogrammetric image consistency, not metric 3D completeness or voxel-level semantic accuracy. The 92% pixel agreement on 135 held-out annotations is useful, but it is still a 2D rendering check of the generated point cloud rather than an independent voxel-level SSC ground-truth audit; it also does not report class-wise accuracy, rare-class behavior, or occupancy false positives/negatives.

Several data-generation choices could introduce systematic label artifacts, but are not ablated: majority-vote tie-breaking by class priors, kNN relabeling with k=100/200, DBSCAN parameters, visual-hull carving with 24 synthetic views, Poisson reconstruction for ground classes, and the fixed instance/other/ground precedence order. These steps can smooth boundaries, hallucinate volume, erase rare classes, or bias labels toward frequent classes, yet the paper treats the generated grids as ground truth.

The dataset is highly imbalanced and small in scene diversity despite many frames. Buildings account for about 62% of overall semantic frequency in Table 7 and 75.7% in the test distribution shown in Table 11, while many classes such as person, bicycle, crane, cable tower, and cable are nearly absent. This weakens claims about a broad 21-class benchmark and makes many class-wise SSC metrics effectively uninformative.

The SSC benchmark is limited. Only two SSC models are evaluated, both adapted from terrestrial settings, and their semantic performance is extremely low: DISC reaches only 2.04% mIoU and Symphonies 0.58% mIoU overall, with many classes at 0%. These results demonstrate difficulty, but they do not provide a strong baseline suite or much insight into which model/design choices matter for aerial SSC.

The depth results are somewhat more convincing, but they are secondary to the SSC contribution. Fine-tuning DepthAnything2 on OccuFly gives strong improvements, yet the paper does not sufficiently separate the value of the depth dataset from the more questionable semantic occupancy benchmark.

The claim of identifying broad failures of 2D and 3D foundation models is overextended. The paper evaluates a small set of pseudo-label/depth models and gives limited detail on adaptation, prompts/settings, or whether stronger aerial-specific segmentation and reconstruction alternatives were considered.

Reproducibility is only partial. The reconstruction relies on Agisoft Metashape 2.2.0, a proprietary tool, and the paper gives limited training hyperparameters for the adapted SSC/depth models. Important details such as annotation guidelines, quality-control procedure, exact split construction, and release/licensing guarantees are not sufficiently specified in the manuscript.

The geographic diversity is limited to the broader Ingolstadt region, with only two test scenes and two validation scenes. The paper frames the benchmark as robust and diverse, but the evidence for generalization across geographies, UAVs, camera intrinsics, urban forms, and capture conditions remains limited.

Overall, the paper has a worthwhile dataset idea, but the reliability of the generated SSC ground truth is the core contribution and is not demonstrated with enough independent evidence. This makes the current acceptance case weak despite the practical motivation and useful preliminary baselines.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear gap: real-world aerial semantic scene completion is underexplored, and OccuFly provides a meaningful new benchmark with 20,611 RGB/voxel/depth samples, 21 semantic classes, three altitudes, multiple environments, and seasonal variation.

The camera-based data generation pipeline is well motivated for UAV settings where LiDAR is often impractical. The use of SfM/MVS, sparse 2D manual annotation, 2D-3D label lifting, class-aware densification, voxelization, and per-frame frustum culling is technically coherent and described in useful detail.

The annotation-efficiency claim is supported by concrete evidence: fewer than 10% of images are manually annotated on average, while reported 2D-3D coverage exceeds 99% of reconstructed points. The supplementary includes per-scene annotation ratios and implementation parameters.

The authors provide several quality checks for the generated data, including reprojection errors, qualitative scene-level visualizations, image overlap analysis, and a held-out render-to-annotation evaluation reporting 92% pixel agreement across 135 manual annotations.

The benchmark experiments are useful even though absolute SSC performance is low: they show a substantial domain gap for existing terrestrial SSC methods and metric depth foundation models, and the depth fine-tuning results demonstrate that the dataset can support practical model adaptation.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and gives enough methodological detail to understand the dataset construction and evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The core ground truth is generated indirectly from photogrammetric reconstruction and lifted 2D labels rather than independently measured 3D occupancy. Reprojection error and rendered 2D agreement are helpful proxies, but they do not fully validate voxel-level occupancy, occluded geometry, or semantic correctness in 3D.

The dataset is still geographically limited: all scenes come from the broader Ingolstadt region, with only 9 scenes total. This weakens claims about broad aerial generalization despite variation in altitude, season, and environment type.

The class distribution is extremely imbalanced, with buildings dominating and several classes nearly absent. The reported SSC mIoU is very low and many rare classes have zero IoU, so the benchmark may be difficult to use for evaluating fine-grained semantic progress without additional class-balanced metrics or protocols.

The SSC benchmarking is relatively narrow, covering only two adapted state-of-the-art methods. More baselines, simpler diagnostic models, or ablations on depth priors would make the conclusions about aerial SSC difficulty more complete.

The data generation pipeline includes many design choices, such as DBSCAN parameters, alpha-shape carving, Poisson reconstruction, class precedence, and kNN relabeling, but the paper provides little ablation or sensitivity analysis showing how these choices affect final voxel quality.

Reproducibility has some limitations because the reconstruction relies on Agisoft Metashape, a proprietary photogrammetry tool, and because release details for code, annotations, and exact processing scripts are not fully established in the manuscript itself.

Some comparisons to terrestrial benchmarks emphasize sample and voxel counts, but OccuFly uses a much coarser voxel size than several driving datasets. These scale comparisons should be interpreted carefully.
